units.title: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data

topics.title: 1.1 Introducing Statistics: What Can We Learn from Data?

outcomes.text: Identify the components of a statistical study
A statistical study collects sample data to answer a question about a larger population
Studies are needed when surveying the whole population is too hard
A datum is one piece of information; many data form a data set
A population is everything of interest; its size is N
A sample is a subset of the population; its size is n
Relate every part of a study and its results to the real-world context ("in context")
Determine an investigative question within a statistical study
A question has a defined purpose and is not changed after seeing results
Pose the question so the needed data can be collected and analysed

topics.title: 1.2 Variables

outcomes.text: Identify observational units, variables, parameters and statistics
An observational unit is an item or individual from which data are collected
A variable is a characteristic that can differ between units
Numerical and categorical data, including images, sounds and text, can carry information
A parameter summarises a variable for a population
A statistic summarises a variable for a sample and is used to infer the parameter
Identify types of variables
Categorical variables take category names or group labels
Quantitative variables take measured or counted numerical values, usually with units
Identify types of quantitative variables
Discrete variables take countable values
Continuous variables take any value within an interval

topics.title: 1.3 Tabular Representation and Summary Statistics for One Categorical Variable

outcomes.text: Construct tables for one categorical variable
A frequency table counts units in each category
A relative frequency table gives the proportion in each category
Describe categorical tables with summary statistics
Percentages, relative frequencies and ratios carry the same information as proportions
Counts and relative frequencies can justify claims in context

topics.title: 1.4 Graphical Representations for One Categorical Variable

outcomes.text: Construct graphs for one categorical variable
Bar charts show frequency or relative frequency per category by bar height
Pie charts show relative frequencies as slice areas totaling 100 percent

subtopics.title: Justifying and comparing with categorical graphs

outcomes.text: Justify a claim using categorical graphs
Graphs of a categorical variable can justify claims in context
Compare multiple categorical tables and graphs
Use tables, bar charts and pie charts to compare data sets on the same categorical variable

topics.title: 1.5 Graphical Representations for One Quantitative Variable

outcomes.text: Construct graphs for one quantitative variable
Histograms, stem-and-leaf plots and dotplots display a distribution in natural order
A histogram groups values into bins whose heights show frequency; bin width changes its look
A stem-and-leaf plot splits each value into stem and leaf, both ordered
A dotplot places one dot per value, stacking near-identical values

topics.title: 1.6 Descriptions for One Quantitative Variable Distributions

outcomes.text: Describe distributions shown in graphs of one quantitative variable
Describe shape, center, variability and unusual features in context
Classify shape as skewed right, skewed left or approximately symmetric
Distinguish unimodal, bimodal and approximately uniform distributions
Outliers are unusually small or large values
A gap is a region with no observed data
Clusters are concentrations of values separated by gaps
Justify a claim using a distribution graph
Graphs of a quantitative variable can justify claims in context

topics.title: 1.7 Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

outcomes.text: Calculate measures of center and position
Mean and median are the common measures of center
The mean is the sum of values divided by their count
The median is the middle value of the ordered data
Minimum and maximum are the smallest and largest values
Quartiles Q1, Q2, Q3 split the ordered data into quarters
The pth percentile has p percent of values at or below it
Calculate measures of variability
Range, IQR and standard deviation measure spread
Range is maximum minus minimum
IQR is Q3 minus Q1
Standard deviation is a typical distance from the mean; its square is the variance
Calculate effects of different units of measurement
Changing measurement units changes the statistics
Calculate outliers
Flag outliers by the 1.5 times IQR rule or by 2 standard deviations from the mean
Compare summary statistics across samples
Compare center, variability, shape and outliers between independent samples
Justify the choice of summary statistic
Median and IQR are resistant to outliers; mean, range and standard deviation are not
Summary statistics can justify claims in context

topics.title: 1.8 Graphical Representations of Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

outcomes.text: Construct graphs of summary statistics
The five-number summary is minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum
A boxplot shows the five-number summary, with whiskers and outliers marked separately
Describe graphs using the mean-median relationship
Symmetric: mean near median; right skew: mean above median; left skew: mean below

topics.title: 1.9 Comparisons of the Distributions for One Quantitative Variable

outcomes.text: Compare graphs of a quantitative variable
Compare center, variability, shape, outliers, clusters and gaps using histograms, dotplots, stem plots and boxplots
Compare graphs of summary statistics
Comparisons can include numerical summaries such as mean and standard deviation
Justify a claim using several graphs
Multiple graphs can justify claims in context
Calculate z-scores using population parameters
A standardised score counts standard deviations from the mean
z equals the value minus the mean, divided by the standard deviation; sample statistics can substitute
Compare z-scores as relative position
Use z-scores to compare positions within or between distributions

topics.title: 1.10 The Investigative Question Revisited and Data Collection

outcomes.text: Determine the components of an investigative question
The first part guides data collection and names the variables
The second part guides the analysis, naming the parameter and the alternative direction or estimation goal
The third part states the population and any cause-and-effect conclusion
Identify a census
A census records information from every unit in the population
Identify an experiment
An experiment assigns treatments to experimental units
The experimental unit is the unit receiving the treatment
Explanatory variables (factors) have levels that are the treatments
The response variable is measured after treatment
Identify an observational study
Observational studies do not impose treatments
Prospective studies gather data now and in the future
Retrospective studies gather past data
A survey asks humans a standard set of questions
A confounding variable linked to both explanatory and response variables offers an alternative explanation
Justify the appropriateness of generalizations
A random sample is chosen by a random mechanism
Random selection allows generalising to the whole population
Volunteer or deliberately chosen samples are not random
Without random selection generalise only to similar individuals

topics.title: 1.11 Random Sampling

outcomes.text: Identify a sampling method from a study description
Sampling without replacement selects each unit at most once
Sampling with replacement can select a unit more than once
In a simple random sample every sample of size n is equally likely
A stratified sample takes a simple random sample from each stratum
A cluster sample randomly selects clusters and surveys everyone in them
A systematic sample uses a random start and fixed interval
Justify the appropriateness of a sampling method
Each method suits different populations and questions

topics.title: 1.12 Potential Problems with Sampling

outcomes.text: Identify potential sources of bias in sampling
Bias is systematic error pushing a statistic consistently high or low
Voluntary response bias arises when the sample is all volunteers
Undercoverage bias arises when part of the population is missed
Nonresponse bias arises when chosen individuals do not respond
Response bias arises from confusing or leading questions or self-reports
Nonrandom methods such as convenience samples risk bias

topics.title: 1.13 Experimental Design

outcomes.text: Identify elements of a well-designed experiment
Include comparison of treatments, random assignment, replication and direct control
A control group provides a comparison, sometimes with a placebo
The placebo effect is the response to a placebo compared with no treatment
In a single-blind experiment only participants or only the research team know the treatments
In a double-blind experiment neither group knows the treatments
An extraneous variable affects the response but is not studied
Random assignment makes treatment groups similar on extraneous variables
A confounding variable is tangled with the explanatory variable; good design reduces it
Replication means more than one unit per treatment
Direct control holds extraneous settings the same across units
Identify experimental designs
In a completely randomized design treatments are assigned entirely at random
A randomized block design groups similar units into blocks and randomises within each
Blocking separates blocking-variable variation to compare treatments more precisely
A matched pairs design is a two-treatment block design on pairs or on repeated units
Justify an experimental design
The best design depends on goals, population, sample and variables
Justify conclusions from an experiment
Random assignment permits cause-and-effect conclusions
When random selection is impractical or unethical, volunteers represent similar units

units.title: Unit 2: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions

topics.title: 2.1 Tabular and Graphical Representations for the Distributions of Two Categorical Variables

outcomes.text: Compare tables and graphs showing the relationship between two categorical variables
A two-way table summarises two categorical variables with counts or proportions
Side-by-side bar charts, segmented bar charts and mosaic plots display two categorical variables
Use these graphs to compare across levels and judge association
Justify a claim using tables and graphs for two categorical variables
These representations can justify claims in context

topics.title: 2.2 Summary Statistics for Two Categorical Variables

outcomes.text: Calculate summary statistics from two-way tables
A joint relative frequency is a cell count over the table total
A marginal relative frequency is a row or column total over the table total
A conditional relative frequency is a cell over its row or column total
Compare summary statistics for two categorical variables
Compare distributions for evidence of association
Justify a claim using summary statistics for two categorical variables
These statistics can justify claims in context

topics.title: 2.3 Estimating Probabilities Using Simulation

outcomes.text: Estimate probabilities using simulations
A random process produces chance results
An outcome is the result of one trial
An event is a collection of outcomes
Simulation models random events and records counts of simulated outcomes
Probability is long-run relative frequency
Empirical relative frequency estimates the true probability
The law of large numbers: relative frequency settles near one value as trials increase

topics.title: 2.4 Introduction to Probability

outcomes.text: Calculate probabilities for events and their complements
The sample space is all nonoverlapping outcomes and has probability 1
With equally likely outcomes, P(E) is outcomes in E over total outcomes
Probabilities lie between 0 and 1
The complement has probability 1 minus P(E)

topics.title: 2.5 Mutually Exclusive Events

outcomes.text: Justify why two events are mutually exclusive using joint probability
Joint probability is the probability of the intersection of A and B
Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together, so P(A and B) is 0

topics.title: 2.6 Conditional Probability

outcomes.text: Calculate conditional probabilities
P(A given B) equals P(A and B) divided by P(B)
The general multiplication rule: P(A and B) equals P(A) times P(B given A)

topics.title: 2.7 Independent Events and Unions of Events

outcomes.text: Calculate probabilities for independent events and for the union of two events
Independent events do not change each other's probabilities, so P(A and B) equals P(A)P(B)
The union is the probability that A or B or both occur
P(A or B) equals P(A) plus P(B) minus P(A and B)

topics.title: 2.8 Introduction to Random Variables and Probability Distributions

outcomes.text: Construct a probability distribution for a discrete random variable
A random variable has numerical values resulting from a random phenomenon
A distribution lists the probability of every value, summing to 1
Build a distribution from probability rules or simulation
Show a distribution as a graph, table or function
A cumulative distribution gives probability of at most each value

topics.title: 2.9 Parameters of Random Variables

subtopics.title: Mean and standard deviation of a random variable

outcomes.text: Calculate the mean and standard deviation for a discrete random variable
A parameter is a single fixed value describing a distribution or population
Expected value is the sum of each value times its probability, the long-run average
Standard deviation is the typical deviation from the expected value; variance is its square
Interpret the mean and standard deviation for a discrete random variable
Interpret them in the context of the population

topics.title: 2.10 The Binomial Distribution

outcomes.text: Justify why a random variable is or is not binomial
Binomial counts successes in n independent trials with two outcomes and success probability p
Calculate the mean and standard deviation for a binomial distribution
The mean is np and the standard deviation is the square root of np(1-p)
Interpret the mean, standard deviation and probabilities for a binomial distribution
Interpret them in context
Estimate binomial probabilities using simulation data
Build a distribution by probability rules or estimate it by simulation
Calculate probabilities for a binomial distribution
Use the binomial probability function for exactly x successes

topics.title: 2.11 The Normal Distribution

outcomes.text: Describe a normal distribution
A continuous random variable takes any value in a domain; intervals carry probability
Many continuous variables are well modelled by a normal distribution
A normal curve is continuous, unimodal, bell-shaped and symmetric
Use a normal curve to model data or a continuous variable
Mean and standard deviation identify a normal curve; larger deviation means a flatter, wider curve
Identify mean and standard deviation of a normal distribution
The standard normal has mean 0 and standard deviation 1
Calculate percentages using the empirical rule
About 68, 95 and 99.7 percent lie within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations of the mean
Calculate the probability of a value in an interval
Probability is the area under the normal curve over the interval; total area is 1
Calculate intervals and areas of a normal distribution
Find interval boundaries for a given area with technology or z-scores and a table
Translate statements about lowest, middle, highest or most extreme p percent into inequalities and areas
Compare measures of relative position
Compare positions using percentiles and proportions within or between normal distributions

topics.title: 2.12 Sampling Distributions and the Central Limit Theorem

outcomes.text: Describe sampling distributions with simulations
A sampling distribution is the distribution of a statistic over all samples of a given size
Simulate it by drawing many random samples and recording the statistic
A randomization distribution comes from repeatedly reassigning responses to treatment groups
The central limit theorem: the sampling distribution of a mean is approximately normal, better with larger samples

units.title: Unit 3: Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions

topics.title: 3.1 Estimators

outcomes.text: Justify why an estimator is or is not unbiased
An estimator is unbiased if on average it neither under- nor overestimates the parameter
Calculate estimates for a population parameter
A sample statistic is a point estimator of its parameter, such as p-hat for p

topics.title: 3.2 Sampling Distributions for Sample Proportions

subtopics.title: Mean and standard deviation of p-hat

outcomes.text: Calculate the mean and standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a sample proportion
With independent values, p-hat has mean p and standard deviation square root of p(1-p)/n
Justify the conditions for the sampling distribution of a sample proportion
Without replacement, check randomization and the 10 percent condition
The distribution is approximately normal when np and n(1-p) are both at least 10
Interpret the mean, standard deviation and probabilities of this sampling distribution
Interpret in the context of the specific population

topics.title: 3.3 Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion

subtopics.title: Choosing the procedure and checking conditions

outcomes.text: Identify the confidence interval procedure and parameter for a proportion
A confidence interval estimates a parameter; use a one-sample z-interval for a proportion
State the parameter with the proportion, response variable and population
Verify conditions for a one-proportion z-interval
Check randomization, 10 percent condition and at least 10 observed successes and failures
Calculate a confidence interval for a population proportion
The critical value z-star bounds the middle C percent of the standard normal
The interval is point estimate plus or minus margin of error

subtopics.title: Standard error and margin of error

outcomes.text: Calculate standard error and margin of error, and estimate a sample size
Standard error estimates the standard deviation of the sampling distribution
Standard error is the typical variation of a statistic from the parameter
Margin of error is the critical value times the standard error
Rearrange the margin-of-error formula to find the minimum n, using 0.5 if p-hat is unknown

topics.title: 3.4 Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion

outcomes.text: Interpret a confidence interval for a population proportion in context
A computed interval may or may not contain the true proportion
Confidence level is the long-run percentage of such intervals that capture the parameter
Say we are C percent confident the interval contains the parameter, stated in context
Justify a claim from a confidence interval
The interval gives plausible values that can support a claim
Identify how sample size, width, confidence level and margin of error relate
Raising the confidence level raises the critical value, margin of error and width
Larger samples lower standard error and narrow the interval, roughly in proportion to one over root n

topics.title: 3.5 Setting Up a Test for a Population Proportion

outcomes.text: Identify the testing method and parameter for a proportion
A hypothesis test makes a decision about a parameter; use a one-sample z-test for a proportion
State the parameter with the proportion, response variable and population
Identify null and alternative hypotheses for a proportion
The null is the status quo assumed unless evidence suggests otherwise; the alternative is the claim under study
The null includes equality; alternatives are one-sided or two-sided
Write H0 as p equals p0 and Ha as p less than, greater than or not equal to p0
Verify conditions for a one-proportion z-test
Check randomization, 10 percent condition and expected successes and failures at least 10

topics.title: 3.6 p-Values

outcomes.text: Interpret the p-value of a test for a proportion
The p-value is the probability, assuming the null is true, of a test statistic as extreme as observed, in the direction of Ha
With a simulated null distribution, the p-value is the proportion of simulated values as extreme
State that the p-value assumes the null hypothesis is true
Small p-values give evidence for the alternative
Large p-values are not evidence for the null

topics.title: 3.7 Carrying Out a Test for a Population Proportion

outcomes.text: Calculate a test statistic and p-value for a proportion
The z-statistic is (p-hat minus p0) over the standard error under the null
The null distribution can be approximated by a probability model such as the standard normal
Find the p-value from the standard normal using a table or technology
Justify a claim from the results of a test for a proportion
The significance level alpha is the preset probability of rejecting a true null
Reject the null if the p-value is below alpha; otherwise fail to reject
Rejecting means convincing evidence for the alternative; failing to reject means not convincing
A test never proves the null true
Test results support answers to the investigative question
State the conclusion in context, tied to the alternative, with non-definitive language

topics.title: 3.8 Potential Errors When Performing Tests

subtopics.title: Type I and Type II errors

outcomes.text: Identify Type I and Type II errors
Type I error: convincing evidence for Ha when Ha is false
Type II error: not convincing evidence for Ha when Ha is true
Power is the probability of correctly rejecting a false null
Calculate the probability of Type I and Type II errors
Type I error probability equals the significance level alpha
Type II error probability is 1 minus power
Identify factors affecting the probability of errors
Type II error falls and power rises with larger samples, smaller standard error, a parameter farther from the null, or larger alpha
Interpret Type I and Type II errors
Either error may be more serious depending on the study
Type I consequences influence the choice of alpha
Type II consequences influence the choice of sample size

topics.title: 3.9 Sampling Distributions for the Difference Between Sample Proportions

outcomes.text: Calculate the mean and standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a difference of two sample proportions
The difference has mean p1 minus p2 and standard deviation from the two variances added
Justify the conditions for this sampling distribution
Check two independent random samples and the 10 percent condition for each
For experiments only random assignment is needed
The distribution is approximately normal when all expected successes and failures are at least 10
Interpret the mean, standard deviation and probabilities
Interpret within the context of the two populations

topics.title: 3.10 Constructing a Confidence Interval for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions

outcomes.text: Identify the interval procedure and parameters for a difference of proportions
Use a two-sample z-interval for a difference between proportions
Parameters refer to the difference, the response variable and the populations
Verify conditions for a two-proportion z-interval
Check randomization, the 10 percent condition (not needed in experiments) and at least 10 observed successes and failures in each sample
Calculate a confidence interval for the difference of two proportions
The point estimate is p1-hat minus p2-hat
The interval is the point estimate plus or minus margin of error
Calculate standard error and margin of error for the difference
Standard error combines the two proportion variances
Margin of error is critical value times standard error

topics.title: 3.11 Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions

outcomes.text: Interpret a confidence interval for a difference of proportions in context
The computed interval may or may not contain the true difference
Confidence level is the long-run percentage of such intervals that capture the difference
State we are C percent confident the interval contains the difference, in context
Justify a claim from the interval
An interval containing 0 gives insufficient evidence of a difference; one without 0 gives sufficient evidence

topics.title: 3.12 Setting Up a Test for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions

outcomes.text: Identify the testing method and parameters for a difference of proportions
Use a two-sample z-test for the difference between proportions
Parameters refer to the population parameters, response variables and populations
Identify null and alternative hypotheses
The null says no difference (p1 equals p2); alternatives are one-sided or two-sided
Verify conditions for a two-proportion z-test
Check randomization, the 10 percent condition and combined-proportion expected counts of at least 10

topics.title: 3.13 Carrying Out a Test for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions

outcomes.text: Calculate the test statistic and p-value for a difference of proportions
The z-statistic uses the pooled proportion and is standard normal under the null
Find the p-value from the standard normal using a table or technology
Interpret the p-value
The p-value assumes the true proportions are equal
Justify a claim from the test
Compare the p-value with alpha to reject or fail to reject
Results support the answer to the investigative question about both populations
State the conclusion in context, tied to Ha, with non-definitive language

topics.title: 3.14 Setting Up a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence

outcomes.text: Describe chi-square distributions
The chi-square statistic measures observed versus expected counts relative to expected counts
Chi-square curves are positive and right-skewed, less so with more degrees of freedom
Identify the testing method for two-way tables
Use a chi-square test for homogeneity to compare distributions across populations
Reference the variable and populations in context
Use a chi-square test for independence to check association within one population
Reference the variables and population in context
Identify hypotheses for chi-square tests
Homogeneity: H0 no difference in distributions; Ha a difference
Independence: H0 no association; Ha an association
Verify conditions for chi-square tests
Check randomization, the 10 percent condition and all expected counts above 5

topics.title: 3.15 Carrying Out a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence

outcomes.text: Calculate expected counts for two-way tables
Expected count is row total times column total over table total
Calculate the chi-square statistic and p-value
Sum observed minus expected squared over expected; df is (rows-1)(columns-1)
Find the p-value from the chi-square distribution
Interpret the p-value
The p-value assumes the null is true
Justify a claim from a chi-square test
Compare the p-value with alpha to reject or fail to reject
Results support the answer to the investigative question
State the conclusion in context, tied to Ha, with non-definitive language

units.title: Unit 4: Inference for Quantitative Data: Means

topics.title: 4.1 Sampling Distributions for Sample Means

subtopics.title: Sampling distribution of a sample mean

outcomes.text: Calculate the mean and standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a sample mean
The sample mean has mean mu and standard deviation sigma over root n
Justify the conditions for the sampling distribution of a sample mean
Check randomization and the 10 percent condition when sampling without replacement
With a normal population, the sample mean is normal at any sample size
Otherwise it is approximately normal when n is at least 30, and more for extreme skew
Interpret the mean, standard deviation and probabilities of this sampling distribution
Interpret in the context of the population

topics.title: 4.2 Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Mean or Population Mean Difference

outcomes.text: Describe t-distributions
t-distributions are symmetric, bell-shaped with heavier tails, set by degrees of freedom, approaching the standard normal as df grows
Use t when sigma is unknown and s must be used
Identify the interval procedure and parameter for a mean or mean difference
Use a one-sample t-interval for a population mean
For matched pairs, take differences and use a one-sample t-interval for the mean difference
State the parameter in context, including the order of subtraction for differences
Verify conditions for a one-sample t-interval
Check randomization, the 10 percent condition, and the sample data condition (normal population, n at least 30, or no strong skew or outliers)
Calculate a confidence interval for a mean or mean difference
The point estimate is the sample mean or mean difference
The interval is x-bar plus or minus t-star times s over root n, with n-1 degrees of freedom
Calculate standard error and margin of error for a one-sample t-interval
Standard error of the mean is s over root n
Margin of error is t-star times the standard error

topics.title: 4.3 Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for a Population Mean or Population Mean Difference

outcomes.text: Interpret a confidence interval for a mean or mean difference in context
The computed interval may or may not contain the true value
Confidence level is the long-run percentage of intervals that capture the parameter
State we are C percent confident the interval contains the parameter, in context
Justify a claim from the interval
The interval gives plausible values that can support a claim
Relate sample size, width, confidence level and margin of error
Higher confidence raises the critical value, margin of error and width
Larger samples shrink standard error and narrow the interval, about one over root n

topics.title: 4.4 Setting Up a Test for a Population Mean or Population Mean Difference

outcomes.text: Identify the testing method and parameter for a mean or mean difference with unknown sigma
Use a one-sample t-test for a population mean
For matched pairs, take differences and use a one-sample t-test for the mean difference
State the parameter in context
Identify null and alternative hypotheses
H0: mu equals mu0, with one-sided or two-sided Ha
For differences, H0: mu-d equals 0, with one-sided or two-sided Ha
Verify conditions for a one-sample t-test
Check randomization, the 10 percent condition and the sample data condition

topics.title: 4.5 Carrying Out a Test for a Population Mean or Population Mean Difference

outcomes.text: Calculate the test statistic and p-value for a mean or mean difference
t equals (x-bar minus mu0) over (s over root n) with n-1 degrees of freedom
Find the p-value from the t-distribution using a table or technology
Interpret the p-value
The p-value assumes the null hypothesis is true
Justify a claim from the test
Reject if the p-value is at most alpha; otherwise fail to reject
Results support the answer to the investigative question
State the conclusion in context, tied to Ha, with non-definitive language

topics.title: 4.6 Sampling Distributions for the Difference Between Two Sample Means

outcomes.text: Calculate the mean and standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a difference of sample means
The difference has mean mu1 minus mu2 and standard deviation root of sigma1 squared over n1 plus sigma2 squared over n2
Justify conditions for this sampling distribution
Check two independent random samples and the 10 percent condition for each
For experiments only random assignment is needed
It is normal if both populations are normal
Otherwise it is approximately normal if both n are at least 30
Interpret the mean, standard deviation and probabilities
Interpret within the context of the specific populations

topics.title: 4.7 Constructing a Confidence Interval for the Difference Between Two Population Means

outcomes.text: Identify the interval procedure and parameter for a difference of means
Use a two-sample t-interval for independent samples
State the parameter as the difference in means, response variable and populations
Verify conditions for a two-sample t-interval
Check randomization, the 10 percent condition (not needed in experiments) and the sample data condition for both samples
Calculate the interval for a difference of means
The point estimate is x1-bar minus x2-bar
The interval is the point estimate plus or minus t-star times the standard error, with df found by technology
Calculate standard error and margin of error for a difference of means
Standard error is root of s1 squared over n1 plus s2 squared over n2
Margin of error is t-star times standard error

topics.title: 4.8 Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for the Difference Between Two Population Means

outcomes.text: Interpret an interval for a difference of means in context
The computed interval may or may not contain the true difference
Confidence level is the long-run capture rate of such intervals
State we are C percent confident the interval contains the difference, in context
Justify a claim from the interval
An interval containing 0 means insufficient evidence of a difference; one without 0 means sufficient evidence

topics.title: 4.9 Setting Up a Test for the Difference Between Two Population Means

outcomes.text: Identify the testing method and parameters for a difference of means
Use a two-sample t-test for a difference between means
Parameters refer to the population parameters, response variables and populations
Identify null and alternative hypotheses
H0: mu1 equals mu2, with one-sided or two-sided Ha
Verify conditions for a two-sample t-test
Check randomization, the 10 percent condition and the sample data condition for both samples

topics.title: 4.10 Carrying Out a Test for the Difference Between Two Population Means

outcomes.text: Calculate the test statistic and p-value for a difference of means
The t-statistic is the observed difference minus the hypothesised difference over the standard error, with df by technology
Find the p-value from the t-distribution
Interpret the p-value
The p-value assumes the population means are equal
Justify a claim from the test
Reject if the p-value is at most alpha; otherwise fail to reject
Results support the answer to the investigative question
State the conclusion in context, tied to Ha, with non-definitive language

topics.title: 5.1 Graphical Representations Between Two Quantitative Variables

outcomes.text: Construct scatterplots of two quantitative variables
Bivariate data are ordered pairs from two quantitative variables on the same individuals
A scatterplot puts the explanatory variable on x and the response on y
Describe the characteristics of a scatterplot
Describe form, direction, strength and unusual features
Form may be linear or non-linear
Direction is positive or negative
Strength is how closely points follow the pattern
Unusual features include clusters and points off the pattern
Justify a claim using scatterplots
Scatterplots can justify claims in context

topics.title: 5.2 Correlation

outcomes.text: Interpret the correlation for a linear relationship
r summarises strength and direction of linear association, is unit-free and lies between -1 and 1
Strength is how close r is to -1 or 1; 0 means no linear association
An r near -1 or 1 does not guarantee a linear model fits
Correlation does not imply causation

topics.title: 5.3 Linear Regression Models

outcomes.text: Calculate a predicted response using a linear regression model
If the relationship looks linear, a regression line predicts y from x
The prediction is y-hat equals a plus bx, with intercept a and slope b
Extrapolation predicts beyond the x-values used and is less reliable
Interpolation predicts within the range of x-values

topics.title: 5.4 Residuals

outcomes.text: Calculate differences between observed and predicted values
A residual is observed minus predicted
Interpret those differences
Positive residuals mean underprediction; negative residuals mean overprediction
Describe the form of association using residual plots
A residual plot graphs residuals against predicted values or the explanatory variable
Residual plots test whether a linear model is appropriate
